title: Quadratic forms
summary: The value x^T A x depends only on the symmetric part of A. That symmetric matrix is positive definite exactly when its eigenvalues are positive, and, for a symmetric matrix, exactly when every leading principal minor is positive.
intuition:
A quadratic form is the scalar $x^\top A x$ for a real column $x$ and a real square matrix $A$. It looks as if every entry of $A$ matters. Only the symmetric part does. Split $A=S+K$ with $S=(A+A^\top)/2$ symmetric and $K=(A-A^\top)/2$ skew-symmetric. The skew piece contributes nothing: $x^\top K x$ is a scalar equal to its own negative, so it is zero. Therefore $x^\top A x=x^\top S x$. Replacing $A$ by $S$ does not change a single value of the form, and it lets every later test assume symmetry.

Positive definite means $x^\top A x>0$ for every $x\neq 0$. Because the form ignores $K$, this happens exactly when every eigenvalue of the symmetric part $S$ is positive. Positive semidefinite is the same sentence with $\ge 0$ and eigenvalues that are nonnegative. One positive and one negative eigenvalue of $S$ makes the form indefinite: some vectors give a positive value and some give a negative value.

Sylvester's criterion is a determinant test, and it needs a symmetric matrix. For a symmetric $n\times n$ matrix, positive definite is equivalent to every leading principal minor being positive: the top-left $1\times 1$, the top-left $2\times 2$, and so on through the whole determinant. The word leading matters. Nonnegative leading minors do not characterize semidefiniteness. And the criterion is not applied to a non-symmetric matrix. If $A$ itself is not symmetric, form $S$ first and test $S$. A matrix can have positive leading minors and still produce a negative value of $x^\top A x$, because those minors were not the minors of $S$.

definitions.body: For a real $n\times n$ matrix $A$ and a column $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the quadratic form is the scalar $x^\top A x$. It equals $x^\top S x$ for the symmetric part $S=(A+A^\top)/2$.

The form is positive definite when $x^\top A x>0$ for every $x\neq 0$, and positive semidefinite when $x^\top A x\ge 0$ for every $x$. Both properties are properties of the symmetric part: they hold exactly when the eigenvalues of $S$ are all positive, or all nonnegative.

The $k$-th leading principal minor of a square matrix is the determinant of its top-left $k\times k$ corner. Sylvester's criterion uses this nested sequence, not an arbitrary collection of principal minors.

Let $A$ be symmetric. Then $A$ is positive definite if and only if every leading principal minor is positive. The matrix in the test must be symmetric. For a non-symmetric matrix, apply the test to $(A+A^\top)/2$.

formulas.name: Quadratic form
formulas.note: Positive definite if and only if every eigenvalue of the symmetric part is positive.

formulas.name: Sylvester's criterion
formulas.note: $A$ must be symmetric. All leading principal minors positive if and only if $A$ is positive definite. Nonnegative leading minors do not characterize positive semidefiniteness.

properties: $x^\top A x=x^\top S x$ with $S=(A+A^\top)/2$. The skew-symmetric part contributes $0$.
A symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if every eigenvalue is positive, and positive semidefinite if and only if every eigenvalue is nonnegative.
Sylvester, symmetric case only: all leading principal minors positive if and only if the matrix is positive definite.

For a symmetric $2\times 2$ matrix, positive definiteness is equivalent to $a_{11}>0$ and $\det A>0$. It is also equivalent to $\mathrm{tr}(A)>0$ and $\det A>0$, because those two conditions force both eigenvalues to be positive.

All leading principal minors merely nonnegative does not imply positive semidefinite. The symmetric matrix $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $0$ and $0$, and $x^\top A x=-x_2^2$ is negative at $(0,1)$.

examples.title: Sylvester and a value, on a symmetric matrix
examples.prompt: Let $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Test positive definiteness by leading minors and by eigenvalues, and compute $x^\top S x$.
steps: The leading minors are $\Delta_1=2>0$ and $\Delta_2=4-1=3>0$. Sylvester's criterion applies because $S$ is symmetric, so $S$ is positive definite.
The characteristic polynomial is $(2-\lambda)^2-1=\lambda^2-4\lambda+3=(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$. The eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$, both positive, which is the same conclusion.
$Sx=(2+2,\ 1+4)^\top=(4,5)^\top$, so $x^\top S x=(1)(4)+(2)(5)=14$. The value is positive, as it must be for a nonzero vector and a positive definite matrix.
examples.answer: $S$ is positive definite. The leading minors are $2$ and $3$, the eigenvalues are $1$ and $3$, and $x^\top S x=14$.

examples.title: Only the symmetric part matters, and Sylvester needs it
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. Compare $x^\top A x$ with the form of the symmetric part, and explain why the leading minors of $A$ do not prove positive definiteness.
steps: The symmetric part is $S=(A+A^\top)/2=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$. The skew part is the rest, $\begin{pmatrix}0&2\\-2&0\end{pmatrix}$.
$Ax=(1-4,\ -1)^\top=(-3,-1)^\top$, so $x^\top A x=-3+1=-2$. And $Sx=(-1,1)^\top$, so $x^\top S x=-1-1=-2$. The two scalars agree, and both are negative.

The leading minors of $A$ itself are $1$ and $\det A=1$, both positive. That does not make the form positive definite: the value at $x$ is $-2$. Sylvester applies to $S$, whose second leading minor is $1-4=-3$, not positive. The eigenvalues of $S$ are $3$ and $-1$, so the form is indefinite.
examples.answer: $x^\top A x=x^\top S x=-2$. Positive leading minors of the non-symmetric matrix $A$ do not imply a positive definite form. The symmetric part is indefinite.

traps: Running Sylvester on a non-symmetric matrix. $\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $1$ and $1$, and $x=(1,-1)^\top$ gives $x^\top A x=-2$. Symmetrize first.

Reading 'all leading principal minors nonnegative' as positive semidefinite. For a symmetric matrix the correct semidefinite test is not that list. $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has nonnegative leading minors and is not positive semidefinite.
Testing only $\det A>0$. For a symmetric $3\times 3$ matrix a positive determinant does not control the two smaller leading minors, so it does not prove positive definiteness.

Keeping the skew-symmetric part in a definiteness calculation. It changes no value of $x^\top A x$. Eigenvalues of $A$ itself, when $A$ is not symmetric, are the wrong list; use the eigenvalues of $(A+A^\top)/2$.
python:
def mulv(A, x):
    return [sum(A[i][j] * x[j] for j in range(len(x))) for i in range(len(A))]

def quad(A, x):
    Ax = mulv(A, x)
    return sum(x[i] * Ax[i] for i in range(len(x)))

S = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]
assert quad(S, [1, 2]) == 14
assert S[0][0] == 2 and S[0][0] * S[1][1] - S[0][1] * S[1][0] == 3
A = [[1, 4], [0, 1]]
Sym = [[1, 2], [2, 1]]
assert quad(A, [1, -1]) == -2
assert quad(Sym, [1, -1]) == -2
assert A[0][0] * A[1][1] - A[0][1] * A[1][0] == 1
assert Sym[0][0] * Sym[1][1] - Sym[0][1] * Sym[1][0] == -3
Bad = [[0, 0], [0, -1]]
assert quad(Bad, [0, 1]) == -1
print(14)

questions.stem: Sylvester's criterion says that a symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if
options: every leading principal minor is positive
every leading principal minor is nonnegative
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. For a symmetric matrix, positive definiteness is equivalent to every leading principal minor being strictly positive. The trace alone, the determinant alone, and the weaker condition that those minors are nonnegative are all strictly less information. The nonnegative list does not even characterize semidefiniteness.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: $x^\top A x$ depends on $A$ only through the symmetric part $(A+A^\top)/2$.
A symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if every eigenvalue is positive.
For a symmetric matrix, all leading principal minors positive is equivalent to positive definite.
For a symmetric matrix, all leading principal minors nonnegative is equivalent to positive semidefinite.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The skew-symmetric part contributes nothing to the form, and for a symmetric matrix the eigenvalue test and Sylvester's leading-minor test both characterize positive definiteness. D is false: $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ has leading minors $0,0$ and takes the value $-1$ at $(0,1)^\top$.

questions.stem: Let $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
options: The leading principal minors are $2$ and $3$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The minors are $2$ and $4-1=3$, both positive, so Sylvester says $S$ is positive definite. The characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$ has roots $1$ and $3$. For the last option, $Sx=(1,-1)^\top$ and $x^\top S x=1+1=2$, not $0$.

questions.stem: Let $S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $x=\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix}$. Enter the integer $x^\top S x$.
questions.solution: The answer is **14**. First $Sx=(4,5)^\top$, because $2\cdot 1+1\cdot 2=4$ and $1\cdot 1+2\cdot 2=5$. Then $x^\top S x=1\cdot 4+2\cdot 5=14$.
